content: 1. Omeprazole, when co-administered with ketoconazole, reduces the levels or effects of ketoconazole by increasing gastric pH. This interaction is relevant only for the oral forms of both drugs. It is recommended to avoid this combination or use an alternative drug. 2. Ketoconazole increases the levels or effects of ondansetron by inhibiting hepatic and intestinal CYP3A4 metabolism. While no dosage adjustment for ondansetron is recommended, close monitoring is advised as CYP450 inhibitors may reduce ondansetron clearance. 3. Ketoconazole elevates the levels or effects of osilodrostat by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Therapy modification is necessary, and the osilodrostat dose should be reduced by half when co-administered with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors. Close monitoring is essential. 4. Ketoconazole increases the levels or effects of osimertinib by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. The clinical significance of this interaction is unclear, but close monitoring is recommended. 5. Ketoconazole raises ospemifene levels by inhibiting both CYP2C9/10 and CYP3A4 metabolism. Caution is advised, and close monitoring is necessary. 6. Oxcarbazepine reduces ketoconazole levels or effects by inducing CYP3A4 metabolism. The clinical significance of this interaction is unclear, but close monitoring is recommended. 7. Ketoconazole increases oxybutynin levels or effects by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Caution is advised, and close monitoring is necessary. 8. Ketoconazole elevates oxycodone levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Therapy modification may be required, and oxycodone dose reduction should be considered when co-administered with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors. Close monitoring is essential. 9. Ketoconazole increases the toxicity of ozanimod by inhibiting BCRP transporters, leading to increased exposure to its active metabolites. This combination should be avoided or an alternative drug should be used. Close monitoring is necessary if co-administration is unavoidable. 10. Ketoconazole raises paclitaxel levels or effects by inhibiting P-glycoprotein (MDR1) efflux transporters and CYP3A4 metabolism. Caution is advised, and close monitoring is necessary. 11. Ketoconazole increases the levels or effects of protein-bound paclitaxel by inhibiting P-glycoprotein (MDR1) efflux transporters and CYP3A4 metabolism. Caution is advised, and close monitoring is necessary. 12. Ketoconazole elevates pacritinib levels or effects by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. This combination is contraindicated. 13. Ketoconazole increases palbociclib levels or effects by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Co-administration with strong CYP3A inhibitors should be avoided. If unavoidable, reduce the palbociclib dose to 75 mg/day. Close monitoring is essential. 14. Ketoconazole raises paliperidone levels or effects by inhibiting P-glycoprotein (MDR1) efflux transporters. Both drugs also prolong the QTc interval. Therapy modification and close monitoring are necessary. 15. Ketoconazole increases palovarotene levels or effects by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. This combination should be avoided or an alternative drug should be used. Close monitoring is necessary. 16. Ketoconazole elevates panobinostat levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. The starting dose of panobinostat should be reduced to 10 mg when co-administered with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors. Close monitoring is essential. 17. Pantoprazole reduces ketoconazole levels or effects by increasing gastric pH. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both drugs. An alternative drug should be considered. 18. Ketoconazole increases pantoprazole levels or effects by inhibiting CYP3A4 and CYP2C19 metabolism. The clinical significance of this interaction is unclear, but close monitoring is recommended. 19. Ketoconazole raises parecoxib levels or effects by inhibiting CYP2C9/10 and CYP3A4 metabolism. Caution is advised, and close monitoring is necessary. 20. Ketoconazole increases paricalcitol levels or effects by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Caution is advised, and close monitoring is necessary. 21. Ketoconazole elevates paromomycin levels or effects by inhibiting P-glycoprotein (MDR1) efflux transporters. However, ketoconazole also decreases paromomycin levels through an unknown mechanism. The clinical significance of this interaction is unclear, but close monitoring is recommended. 22. Ketoconazole and paroxetine both prolong the QTc interval. Therapy modification and close monitoring are necessary. 23. Ketoconazole and pazopanib both prolong the QTc interval. Ketoconazole also increases pazopanib levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Co-administration should be avoided if possible. If unavoidable, reduce the pazopanib dose to 400 mg/day. Close monitoring is essential. 24. Ketoconazole increases pemigatinib levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Co-administration with strong or moderate CYP3A4 inhibitors should be avoided. If unavoidable, reduce the pemigatinib dose as per the drug monograph. After discontinuing the CYP3A4 inhibitor, resume the previous pemigatinib dose. Close monitoring is necessary. 25. Ketoconazole and pentamidine both prolong the QTc interval. This combination is contraindicated. 26. Pentobarbital reduces ketoconazole levels or effects by inducing CYP3A4 metabolism and inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both drugs. The clinical significance of this interaction is unclear, but close monitoring is recommended. 27. Ketoconazole increases perampanel levels or effects by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Caution is advised, and close monitoring is necessary. 28. Ketoconazole and perphenazine both prolong the QTc interval. This combination should be avoided or an alternative drug should be used. 29. Ketoconazole increases pexidartinib levels or effects by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism and UGT enzymes. Co-administration should be avoided. If unavoidable, reduce the pexidartinib dose as per the drug monograph. Pexidartinib can cause hepatotoxicity, so avoid combining it with other hepatotoxic agents. Close monitoring is essential. 30. Phenobarbital reduces ketoconazole levels or effects by inducing CYP3A4 metabolism and inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both drugs. The clinical significance of this interaction is unclear, but close monitoring is recommended. 31. Ketoconazole increases phenytoin levels or effects by inhibiting CYP2C9/10 metabolism. Conversely, phenytoin reduces ketoconazole levels by inducing CYP3A4 metabolism. The clinical significance of this interaction is unclear, but close monitoring is recommended. 32. Ketoconazole elevates pimavanserin levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Co-administration should be avoided. If unavoidable, reduce the pimavanserin dose to 10 mg/day. Close monitoring is necessary. 33. Ketoconazole and pimozide both prolong the QTc interval. Ketoconazole also increases pimozide levels by inhibiting its metabolism. This combination is contraindicated. 34. Ketoconazole increases pioglitazone levels or effects by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Caution is advised, and close monitoring is necessary. 35. Ketoconazole raises piroxicam levels or effects by inhibiting CYP2C9/10 metabolism. The clinical significance of this interaction is unclear, but close monitoring is recommended. 36. Ketoconazole increases pirtobrutinib levels or effects by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Co-administration should be avoided. If unavoidable, reduce the pirtobrutinib dose by 50 mg. If the current dose is 50 mg/day, discontinue pirtobrutinib during the use of strong CYP3A inhibitors. After discontinuing the inhibitor, resume the previous pirtobrutinib dose. Close monitoring is essential. 37. Ketoconazole increases pitavastatin toxicity by inhibiting OATP1B1 transporters, which may increase the risk of myopathy. Caution is advised, and close monitoring is necessary. 38. Ketoconazole elevates polatuzumab vedotin levels or effects by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Co-administration with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors may increase polatuzumab vedotin toxicities. Caution is advised, and close monitoring is necessary. 39. Ketoconazole increases pomalidomide levels by inhibiting CYP1A2 metabolism and P-glycoprotein (MDR1) efflux transporters. This combination should be avoided or an alternative drug should be used. 40. Ketoconazole raises ponatinib levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Co-administration should be avoided. If unavoidable, reduce the ponatinib starting dose to 30 mg/day. Close monitoring is essential. 41. Ketoconazole increases posaconazole levels or effects by inhibiting P-glycoprotein (MDR1) efflux transporters. Both drugs also prolong the QTc interval. Conversely, posaconazole increases ketoconazole levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. The clinical significance of this interaction is unclear, but close monitoring is recommended. 42. Ketoconazole elevates pralsetinib levels or effects by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism and P-glycoprotein (MDR1) efflux transporters. Co-administration should be avoided. If unavoidable, reduce the pralsetinib dose as per the drug monograph. After discontinuing the inhibitors, resume the previous pralsetinib dose. Close monitoring is necessary. 43. Ketoconazole increases pravastatin toxicity by inhibiting OATP1B1 transporters, which may increase the risk of myopathy. Caution is advised, and close monitoring is necessary. 44. Ketoconazole raises praziquantel levels or effects by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Caution is advised, and close monitoring is necessary. 45. Ketoconazole increases prednisolone levels or effects by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism and P-glycoprotein (MDR1) efflux transporters. Caution is advised, and close monitoring is necessary. 46. Ketoconazole elevates prednisone levels or effects by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism and P-glycoprotein (MDR1) efflux transporters. Co-administration should be avoided. If unavoidable, close monitoring is necessary. 47. Ketoconazole and pretomanid both increase each other's toxicity. Pretomanid is associated with hepatotoxicity. This combination should be avoided, and hepatotoxic agents, including alcohol and herbal supplements, should be avoided during pretomanid therapy. 48. Primidone reduces ketoconazole levels or effects by inducing CYP3A4 metabolism and inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both drugs. The clinical significance of this interaction is unclear, but close monitoring is recommended. 49. Ketoconazole and procainamide both prolong the QTc interval. This combination is contraindicated. 50. Ketoconazole and prochlorperazine both prolong the QTc interval. This combination should be avoided or an alternative drug should be used. 51. Ketoconazole increases progesterone levels or effects (intravaginal gel, micronized, or natural forms) by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Caution is advised, and close monitoring is necessary. 52. Ketoconazole and promazine both prolong the QTc interval. This combination should be avoided or an alternative drug should be used. 53. Ketoconazole and promethazine both prolong the QTc interval. This combination should be avoided or an alternative drug should be used. 54. Ketoconazole elevates propafenone levels or effects by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Caution is advised, and close monitoring is necessary. 55. Ketoconazole and protriptyline both prolong the QTc interval. This combination should be avoided or an alternative drug should be used. 56. Ketoconazole increases quetiapine levels or effects by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. The quetiapine dose should be reduced to one-sixth of the original dose when co-administered with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors. Close monitoring is essential. 57. Ketoconazole and quinidine both prolong the QTc interval. Ketoconazole also increases quinidine levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. This combination is contraindicated. 58. Ketoconazole raises quinine levels or effects by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Caution is advised, and close monitoring is necessary.
